chapter: The Latin scene and business of the 1940s-70s
title: Palladium in the 1950s and Tito Puente's album
summary: The Palladium's three bands and a hit by another bandleader.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: What did you think of the band of the '50s? You played the high days of the Palladium, when there were three bands playing, right?

Yeah, he had a good band, no question about it. He had a good band. Yes, I remember. His band worked there, Rodriguez did his work for (unintelligible). Some way, he got away from New York for one reason or another, or he got lucky. (Unintelligible) came to me and said, I want your band. I say, I still got one more year to go. I think I was (inaudible), or Columbia, one of them. I got one more year to go on my contract but (inaudible). And the record they made, they made live right there at the Palladium.
All right, so they made about two or three albums.
I guess what they expect came up. So --
(Unintelligible) of the band to create their sound. So they give me notice, said you got one more album and this is it.

So (unintelligible). The man in charge of recording that band was -- what's the name of this fellow? His arrangements -- Leroy Holmes. (Unintelligible) got ahold of Tito and says, Tito, this is your last album. I wish you'd let me do something. Get yourself about ten good boleros, bring them to me and let me write it and make the arrangement, get the type of thing I want them to do. (Inaudible.) There's only one more album, anyhow.

See, what happened, they recorded the album, they had a tune in there about (unintelligible). That tune hit in Buenos Aires and from Buenos Aires all the way back over here. And from then on, that band made some money.
Yeah, really as a sort of a singer, huh?
